vjimc-1997-cat2-01.title: An explicit family of skew lines
vjimc-1997-cat2-01.body:
**Yes.** For $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$ let $p_{a,b}$ be the line through $A_{a,b}=(a,b,0)$ with direction $s_{a,b}=(-b,a,1)$:
$$p_{a,b}=\{(a-tb,\ b+ta,\ t):t\in\mathbb R\}.$$
Note that the parameter $t$ equals the $z$-coordinate.

**The lines cover space.** Given $X=(x,y,z)$ we need $a-zb=x$ and $b+za=y$. This linear system in $(a,b)$ has determinant $1+z^2\ne0$, with the unique solution
$$a=\frac{x+yz}{1+z^2},\qquad b=\frac{y-xz}{1+z^2}.$$
So $X\in p_{a,b}$ for exactly one pair $(a,b)$.

**Distinct lines are skew.** Let $(a,b)\ne(c,d)$.
- *They do not meet:* a common point would have the same $z$-coordinate, hence the same parameter $t=z$ on both lines. By uniqueness in the previous paragraph, a point determines $(a,b)$, so $(a,b)=(c,d)$. (Directly: $a-c=t(b-d)$ and $b-d=-t(a-c)$ give $(a-c)^2+(b-d)^2=0$.)
- *They are not parallel:* the directions $(-b,a,1)$ and $(-d,c,1)$ both have third coordinate $1$, so they are proportional only if equal, i.e. $(a,b)=(c,d)$.

Two lines in space that neither meet nor are parallel are not coplanar. So $\{p_{a,b}\}$ is a covering of $\mathbb R^3$ by pairwise skew lines.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-02.title: Blaschke product and the maximum principle
vjimc-1997-cat2-02.body:
Let $\Delta=\{|z|<1\}$. Since $|f|=1$ on $|z|=1$, $f\not\equiv0$ and $f$ has no zeros on the unit circle. $f$ has only finitely many zeros in $\overline\Delta$: otherwise they would accumulate in the compact set $\overline\Delta$, and the identity theorem would give $f\equiv0$. Let $z_1,\dots,z_n\in\Delta$ be these zeros, listed with multiplicity ($n=0$ is allowed).

**Blaschke product.** Let
$$B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{z-z_j}{1-\overline{z_j}z}.$$
Each factor is holomorphic except for a pole at $1/\overline{z_j}$ (outside $\overline\Delta$; no pole if $z_j=0$). For $|z|=1$ we have $|1-\overline{z_j}z|=|\overline z-\overline{z_j}|\,|z|=|z-z_j|$, so each factor has modulus $1$ on the circle.

**The quotient $g=f/B$.** The zeros of $B$ in $\overline\Delta$ are exactly the $z_j$, with the same multiplicities as for $f$. So $g$ extends holomorphically to a disc $|z|<\rho$ with $\rho>1$, and $g$ has no zeros in $\overline\Delta$. On $|z|=1$, $|g|=|f|/|B|=1$.

By the maximum principle, $|g|\le1$ on $\overline\Delta$. Since $g$ has no zeros there, $1/g$ is holomorphic, and the maximum principle applied to $1/g$ gives $|g|\ge1$. Thus $|g|\equiv1$ on $\Delta$. A holomorphic function of constant modulus on a domain is constant (open mapping theorem), so $g\equiv e^{i\theta}$ for some $\theta\in\mathbb R$. Hence
$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}B(z)\quad\text{on }\Delta,$$
and by the identity theorem on $\mathbb C$ minus the poles of $B$.

**All zeros are at $0$.** Suppose some $z_j\ne0$. Then $B$ has a pole at $w=1/\overline{z_j}$. The numerator factors $z-z_i$ vanish only at the points $z_i\in\Delta$, and $|w|>1$, so this pole is not cancelled. Hence $|f(z)|=|B(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to w$, contradicting the continuity of the entire function $f$ at $w$. Therefore $z_1=\dots=z_n=0$, so $B(z)=z^n$, and
$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}z^k\qquad(k=n)$$
on $\mathbb C\setminus\{\text{poles}\}=\mathbb C$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-02.title: Reflection: $f$ is a polynomial
vjimc-1997-cat2-02.body:
**Reflection identity.** Define $h(z)=\overline{f(1/\overline z)}$ for $z\ne0$; it is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. On $|z|=1$ we have $1/\overline z=z$, so $h(z)=\overline{f(z)}=1/f(z)$. Thus $f(z)h(z)=1$ on the unit circle. By the identity theorem, $f(z)h(z)=1$ for all $z\ne0$.

**$f$ is a polynomial.** In particular $f$ has no zeros in $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. Write $f(z)=z^kf_1(z)$ with $f_1$ entire and $f_1(0)\ne0$; then $f_1$ has no zeros at all. For $|z|\ge1$, put $u=1/\overline z$ with $|u|\le1$. Then
$$|f(z)|=\frac1{|h(z)|}=\frac1{|f(u)|}\le\frac1{m},\qquad m=\min_{0<|u|\le1}|f(u)|\cdot\ldots$$
To avoid the zero at $u=0$, use $f_1$ instead: on $|z|\ge1$,
$$|f_1(z)|=\frac{|f(z)|}{|z|^k}=\frac{1}{|z|^k|f(u)|}=\frac{1}{|z|^k|u|^k|f_1(u)|}=\frac1{|f_1(u)|}\le\frac1{\mu},$$
where $\mu=\min_{|u|\le1}|f_1(u)|>0$ and we used $|zu|=1$. So $f_1$ is bounded on $|z|\ge1$, and also on the compact disc $|z|\le1$. By Liouville's theorem $f_1$ is a constant $c$.

**Conclusion.** $f(z)=cz^k$, and $|f|=1$ on the circle gives $|c|=1$, i.e. $c=e^{i\theta}$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-03.title: Integrate by parts, then a weighted AM-GM
vjimc-1997-cat2-03.body:
**Green's identity.** Apply the divergence theorem to the $C^1(\overline D)$ vector field $u\nabla u$. Its divergence is $\operatorname{div}(u\nabla u)=|\nabla u|^2+u\,\Delta u$. Hence
$$\int_D|\nabla u|^2\,dV+\int_Du\,\Delta u\,dV=\int_{\partial D}u\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\,dS=0,$$
because $u=0$ on $\partial D$. So
$$\int_D|\nabla u|^2\,dV=-\int_Du\,\Delta u\,dV\le\int_D|u|\,|\Delta u|\,dV .$$

**Pointwise inequality.** For $\varepsilon>0$ and real $s,t$,
$$|s|\,|t|\le\varepsilon t^2+\frac{s^2}{4\varepsilon},\quad\text{since}\quad \varepsilon t^2+\frac{s^2}{4\varepsilon}-|s||t|=\left(\sqrt\varepsilon\,|t|-\frac{|s|}{2\sqrt\varepsilon}\right)^2\ge0 .$$
With $s=u$, $t=\Delta u$ and integrating,
$$\int_D|\nabla u|^2\,dV\le\varepsilon\int_D(\Delta u)^2\,dV+\frac1{4\varepsilon}\int_Du^2\,dV .$$
∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-03.title: Cauchy-Schwarz and optimising over $\varepsilon$ (official approach)
vjimc-1997-cat2-03.body:
Write $I_\Delta=\int_D(\Delta u)^2\,dV$ and $I_0=\int_Du^2\,dV$. As in the first approach, $\int_D|\nabla u|^2=-\int_Du\,\Delta u$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
$$\int_D|\nabla u|^2\,dV\le\sqrt{I_\Delta I_0}.$$
For every $\varepsilon>0$, AM-GM gives
$$\varepsilon I_\Delta+\frac{I_0}{4\varepsilon}\ge2\sqrt{\varepsilon I_\Delta\cdot\frac{I_0}{4\varepsilon}}=\sqrt{I_\Delta I_0}.$$
Equality holds at $\varepsilon=\frac12\sqrt{I_0/I_\Delta}$ when $I_\Delta>0$; this is the minimum of the right-hand side over $\varepsilon$. Combining the two inequalities gives the claim for every $\varepsilon>0$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-04m.title: Roots-of-unity filter
vjimc-1997-cat2-04m.body:
**Step 1: rewrite the left side.** Since $(7n)^2=7n(7n-1)+7n$,
$$\frac{n^2}{(7n)!}=\frac1{49}\cdot\frac{7n(7n-1)+7n}{(7n)!}=\frac1{49}\left(\frac1{(7n-2)!}+\frac1{(7n-1)!}\right)\qquad(n\ge1).$$
Hence
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n^2}{(7n)!}=\frac1{49}\sum_{k=1}^2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{(7n-k)!}.$$

**Step 2: the filter.** Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/7}$. For an integer $N$, $\sum_{j=0}^6\omega^{jN}$ equals $7$ if $7\mid N$; otherwise it is the geometric sum $\frac{\omega^{7N}-1}{\omega^N-1}=0$. Using $e^{\omega^j}=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{\omega^{jm}}{m!}$ (a finite sum over $j$ of absolutely convergent series, so we may interchange):
$$\sum_{j=0}^6\omega^{jk}e^{\omega^j}=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{m!}\sum_{j=0}^6\omega^{j(m+k)}=7\sum_{\substack{m\ge0\\ m\equiv-k\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 7)}}\frac1{m!}.$$
For $k=1,2$, the integers $m\ge0$ with $m\equiv-k\pmod7$ are exactly $m=7n-k$ with $n\ge1$. So
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{(7n-k)!}=\frac17\sum_{j=0}^6\omega^{jk}e^{\omega^j}\qquad(k=1,2).$$

**Step 3: real parts.** We have $\omega^{jk}e^{\omega^j}=e^{\cos(2\pi j/7)}\,e^{i\left(\sin(2\pi j/7)+2\pi jk/7\right)}$. The left side of Step 2 is real, so it equals its real part:
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{(7n-k)!}=\frac17\sum_{j=0}^6e^{\cos(2\pi j/7)}\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi j}7+\sin\frac{2\pi j}7\right).$$
Combining with Step 1 (factor $\frac1{49}\cdot\frac17=\frac1{7^3}$) gives the identity. (Numerically both sides equal $0.000198412744\ldots$; the $n=1$ term $1/7!$ dominates.) ∎

vjimc-1997-cat2-04i.title: Diagonalise with the Recursion Theorem
vjimc-1997-cat2-04i.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that a program *Gen-Test-Data* computing $P\mapsto D(P)$ exists.

**The transformation.** Let *Transf* be the program that, given (the text of) a program $P$, outputs the text of the following program $P'$:

```
s := input;
compute D := Gen-Test-Data(P);      { the text of P is built into P' }
if s is in D then
    output yes/no according to whether s is the binary code of a multiple of 3
else
    output yes
```

*Transf* is a legitimate program: it only pastes the text of $P$ into a fixed template. $P'$ always halts, since *Gen-Test-Data* halts with a finite set, membership in a finite set is decidable, and *Div₃* is decidable.

**The fixed point.** By the Recursion Theorem there is a program $P_0$ with the same input/output behaviour as $P_0'=\textit{Transf}(P_0)$. So on input $s$, $P_0$ answers correctly if $s\in D(P_0)$ and answers *yes* otherwise.

**Contradiction.**
- $P_0$ gives the correct answer on every input from $D(P_0)$. By the specification of *Gen-Test-Data*, $P_0$ solves *Div₃*.
- But $D(P_0)$ is finite, while there are infinitely many strings coding numbers not divisible by 3, e.g. $1, 10, 100, 1000,\dots$ (the powers of $2$). Take such a string $s\notin D(P_0)$. Then $P_0$ outputs *yes* on $s$, which is wrong, so $P_0$ does not solve *Div₃*.

This contradiction shows that no program *Gen-Test-Data* exists. ∎
